about.title: About
lines: Wikimedia publishes how often every Wikipedia article is read, every hour.
Looked Up reads the 30 largest editions, which carry 98.5 % of human article views.
Each article is compared with its own last 28 days at the same hour.
A spike is a sudden jump far above that baseline.
Wikidata joins the same topic across languages, so Lisbon, Lisboa and リスボン count as one.
An event is one topic spiking in two languages or more within six hours.
Tiers say how far it spread: noticed (2+), international (5+), planetary (20+).
It updates every hour, about three hours behind real time, because that is when the data is published.
limits: Delay: Wikimedia publishes each hour about two hours after it ends, so the newest events are about three hours old.
Languages, not countries: a spike in Spanish could come from Mexico, Spain or the United States.
Fame bias: widely known people and spectacles spread; local news rarely leaves its language.
30 languages: they carry 98.5 % of human views, but entire communities beyond them are invisible here.
about.dataset: the open dataset on Hugging Face
about.privacy: No cookies, no tracking. Your theme and language choice stay in your browser.
about.live: Editors follow readers: in 2,000 September–October events, edit bursts came a median 1 h 46 min after the first reading spike, yet about 1 h 26 min before the pageview numbers were published.

forecast.note: Forecast from a model trained on past events; backtested AUC {auc}.
forecast.title: Forecast
forecast.auc: AUC on 17 unseen days: does it rank events that go international?
forecast.lift: more international events among the top 10 % of forecasts
forecast.gain: smaller error than a simple decay rule, for the attention left in the next 24 hours
forecast.chart: Predicted probability (across) against what happened (up), test days; dot size = number of events
forecast.summary: An hour after an event is first seen in two languages, the model sorts the ones that will reach five languages well (AUC {auc} on 17 days it never saw), and its probabilities are roughly honest, slightly overconfident in the middle. Fame alone is not enough: how many Wikipedias have an article explains only a fifth of what the model knows. What matters most is how much reading is already happening, how wide it already is, and the hour of the day. It predicts the attention left in the next 24 hours better than a simple decay rule, but not the moment attention fades. Planetary forecasts rest on very few past cases and are shown only above 30 %.
